label: properties
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{properties}   Let $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure and  $p:\Omega\to [1,+\infty]$  an exponent function
 such that $p_+(\Omega\setminus\Omega_\infty)<\infty$.  Then, the following properties are all satisfied  for every $f\in L^{p(\cdot)}(\Omega)$:




(1)  $\rho(f/\Vert f\Vert)=1$. In particular $\rho(f)\leq 1$ if and only if $\Vert f\Vert\leq 1$

(2) The convergence in modulus for $\rho(\cdot)$ is equivalent to the norm convergence.

label: PS

label: Sch
title: Example
body_md:
\label{Sch}

Let  $X$ be a Banach space endowed with a Schauder basis $(e_n)_n$.  The family $\mathcal{P}$ consisting of the canonical projections $P_n:X\to X$, defined   by $P_n(\sum_{k=1}^\infty x_k e_k)=\sum_{k=1}^n x_k e_k$  together with  $P_\omega=I$  is a projection scheme on $X$.
head: environment

label: VLSPS
title: Example
body_md:
\label{VLSPS}

Let $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a  $\sigma$-finite measure space.  Let $p: \Omega\to (1,+\infty)$ be a measurable function such that  $1=p_-(\Omega)<p_+(\Omega)<\infty$. Fix a nonincreasing sequence $(\gamma_n)\subset (1,+\infty)$  with $\lim_n\gamma_n=1$. For $n\in\mathbb{N}$, define $P_n: L^{p(\cdot)}(\Omega)\to L^{p(\cdot)}(\Omega)$ by $P_n(f)=f\cdot \chi_{p^{-1}(\gamma_n,\infty)}$ and $P_\omega=I$.  Then $\mathcal{P}=\{P_n: 1\le n\le \omega\}$ is a PS on $L^{p(\cdot)}(\Omega)$. More details, together with a slight modification of this construction, will be given in Section \ref{VLSsection}).
head: environment

label: Pconvergence
title: Definition
body_md: \label{Pconvergence} Let $\mathcal{P}=\{ P_k: 1\le k\le \omega\}$ be a projection scheme on  $X$.  We say that a  sequence $(x_n)_n$ in $X$ is $\mathcal{P}$-convergent to some $x\in X$, denoted by $\mathcal{P}-\lim_n x_n=x$,  if $\lim_n P_k(x_n)=P_k(x)$ for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\lim_n (I-P_\omega)(x_n)=(I-P_\omega)(x)$.
head: environment

label: PS2
title: Definition
head: environment

label: kUC
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{kUC}
Let $A:X\to X$ be a  bounded operator. We say that $X$ is $A$-uniformly convex ($A$-UC) if for all $\epsilon>0$, there exists some $\gamma(A)>0$ such that for all $x,y\in B_X$  either
$$
\Vert A(x-y)\Vert<\epsilon \mbox{ or }\left\Vert {x+y\over 2}\right\Vert<1-\gamma(A).$$

If $\mathcal{A}=\{A_n: n\in\mathbb{N}\}$ is a family of linear bounded operators from $X$ into $X$, we say that $X$ is $\mathcal{A}$-UC if $X$ is $A_n$-UC for all $A_n\in\mathcal{A}$.
head: environment

label: puc
title: Example
body_md:
\label{puc}
Let $X=Y\oplus_2 Z$ where $Y$ is uniformly convex, $Z$ is any Banach space and the norm on $X$  is given by $\Vert x\Vert_X:=\left(\Vert y\Vert_Y^2+\Vert z\Vert_Z^2\right)^{1\over 2}$ if $x=y+z$ with $y\in Y$ and $z\in Z$.
Define $A:X\to X$ given by $A(x)=y$ if $x=y+z$. Then $X$ is $A$-UC.

\medskip


Indeed, fix some $\epsilon>0$ and $x_1,x_2\in B_X$ with $x_i=y_i+z_i$, $y_i\in Y$, $z_i\in Z$, $i=1,2$ and assume that $\Vert y_1-y_2\Vert\ge \epsilon$. Using that $Y$ is UC, there exists some $\delta_Y(\epsilon)$ such that \cite[Proposition 1, page 190]{Bea}:
$$
\left\Vert{y_1+y_2\over 2}\right\Vert_Y^2\le {\Vert y_1\Vert^2+\Vert y_2\Vert_Y^2\over 2}-\delta_Y(\epsilon).
$$
By the convexity of the function $\Vert \cdot\Vert^2$, when $\Vert\cdot\Vert$ is any norm, we have
$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\left\Vert {x_1+x_2\over 2}\right\Vert_X^2&\le& {\Vert y_1\Vert_Y^2+\Vert y_2\Vert_Y^2\over 2}-\delta_Y(\epsilon)+ {\Vert z_1\Vert_Z^2+\Vert z_2\Vert_Z^2\over 2}\\
  &= & {\Vert x_1\Vert^2_X+\Vert x_2\Vert_X^2\over 2}-\delta_Y(\epsilon).\\
  \end{array}
$$
Taking square root and adjusting the coefficients we obtain  that Definition \ref{kUC} is satisfied.
head: environment

label: AUC
title: Definition
head: environment

label: ac
title: Definition
body_md: \label{ac} Let $X$ be a Banach space endowed with a metrizable topo\-logy $\tau$. We say that a nonincreasing  sequence  $\{Z_s: s\in\mathbb{N}\}$ of closed bounded subsets in $X$ is $\tau$-asymptotically compact if for every sequence $(z_s)\subset X$ with $z_s\in Z_s$ for $s\in\mathbb{N}$,  there exists a $\tau$-convergent subsequence.
head: environment

label: Pasymp
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
When $(Z_s)$ is $\mathcal{P}$-asymptotically compact, it can  be easily checked that  $\lim_s\alpha(P_n(Z_s))=0$ para todo $n\in\mathbb{N}$ (without the requirement of being boundedly complete).

\medskip

Let us prove the converse: 
Let $(z_s)$ be a sequence in $X$, with $z_s\in Z_s$ for every $s\in\mathbb{N}$. Since $(I-P_\omega)$ has finite rank, we can assume, without loss of generality,  that there exists some $v_0\in (I-P_\omega)(X)$ such that $\lim_s (I-P_\omega)(z_s)=v_0$

Let $(\epsilon_k)$ be a nonnegative null sequence. Using a diagonal argument, we can construct a subsequence $(s_k)_k$ such that
$$
\alpha\left(P_k(Z_{s_k})\right)<\epsilon_k
$$
for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$. We prove that $\alpha(\{P_n(z_{s_k}):k\in\mathbb{N}\})=0$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Indeed, fix $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Take  $j>n$.
Then
$
\alpha(\{P_n(z_{s_k}):k\in\mathbb{N}\})=\alpha(\{P_n(z_{s_k}): s_k\ge s_j\})$. For $k,k^\prime$ with $s_k, s_{k^\prime}\ge s_j$ we have:
$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\Vert P_n(z_{s_k})-P_n(z_{s_{k^\prime}})\Vert & = & \Vert P_nP_j(z_{s_k})-P_nP_j(z_{s_{k^\prime}})\Vert\\
 & \le & {K}(\mathcal{P})\Vert P_j(z_{s_k})-P_j(z_{s_{k^\prime}})\Vert.
 \end{array}
$$
Therefore:
$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\alpha(\{P_n(z_{s_k}): s_k\ge s_j\})& \le& {K}(\mathcal{P})\alpha\left(\{P_{j}(z_{s_k}): s_k\ge s_j\}\right)\\
 & \le &  \mathcal{K}(\mathcal{P} )\alpha(P_j(Z_{s_{j}}))\le \epsilon_j.\\
\end{array}
$$
Consequently $\alpha(\{P_n(z_{s_k}):k\in\mathbb{N}\})=0$.  Taking a diagonal argument, we can assume, up to a subsequence,  that  $\{P_n(z_{s})\}_s$ is norm-convergent for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Then, there is a further sequence $(u_n)$ such that
$$
\lim_s\Vert P_n(z_s)-u_n\Vert=0\ \forall n\in\mathbb{N}.
$$
In particular $(u_n)$ is norm-bounded.
Take $n\le m<\omega$. We have
$$
P_n(u_m)=\lim_s P_nP_m(z_s)=\lim_s P_n(z_s)=u_n.
$$


Since $\mathcal{P}$ is boundedly complete, there exists $v_1\in P_\omega(X)$ with $P_n(v_1)=u_n$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$,   which implies  that $\lim_s P_n(z_s)=P_n(v_1)$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Since $v_1\in P_\omega(X)$ and $v_0\in (I-P_\omega)(X)$, the above implies that the sequence $(z_s)$ is $\mathcal{P}$-convergent to the vector $v_1+v_0\in X$ and the proof is complete.
head: environment

label: gamma
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{gamma}
Let $X$ be a Banach space. Let $A:X\to X$ be a linear bounded operator and assume that   $X$ is $A$-UC.
Let $C$ be a closed convex bounded subset and $(x_k)$ a sequence in $C$. Then
$$
\lim_{\delta\to 0^+}{\rm diam} \left[A(Z(\{x_k\},C,\delta))\right]=0.
$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In case that $r(\{x_k)\},C)=0$, the sequence $(x_n)$ converges to some $x\in C$ and $\{x\}=Z(\{x_k\},C)$. Thus  $Z(\{x_k\},C,\delta)$ is contained in a ball centered at $x$ with radius $\delta$ and there is nothing to prove. Set $r:=r(\{x_k\},C)>0$.

Fix some $n\in\mathbb{N}$. 
Assume,  to the contrary, that there exists some $c>0$ such that:
$$
 0<c< \inf_{\delta>0}{\rm diam} \left[A(Z(\{x_k\},C,\delta))\right]=\lim_{\delta\to 0^+}{\rm diam}\left[A(Z(\{x_k\},C,\delta))\right]
$$
  For $\epsilon:=\frac{c}{ r+1}>0$ consider the corresponding  $\gamma(A)>0$ stated in the Definition \ref{kUC}. Find some $0<\delta<1$ such that $(r+\delta)(1-\gamma(A))<r$.

\medskip

Since $c<{\rm diam} \left[A(Z(\{x_k\},C,\delta/2))\right]$, we can find two points $y_1, y_2\in Z(\{x_k\},C,\delta/2)$ such that $\Vert  A(y_1-y_2)\Vert \geq c$.

 Then, there exists $k_0\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for all $k\ge k_0$:
 $$
 \Vert x_k-y_1\Vert \le r+\delta,\qquad \Vert x_k-y_2\Vert\le r+\delta.
 $$
For $k\ge k_0$, define $\displaystyle{u_k:=\frac{x_k-y_1}{ r+\delta}}$, $\displaystyle{v_k:=\frac{x_k-y_2}{ r+\delta}}$. Then, $\Vert u_k\Vert \le 1$, $\Vert v_k\Vert \le 1$ and $\Vert A(u_k-v_k)\Vert\ge \frac{c}{ r+\delta}>\frac{c}{ r+1}$. Thus,
$$
\left\Vert x_k-\frac{y_1+y_2}{ 2}\right\Vert=(r+\delta)\left\Vert \frac{u_k+v_k}{ 2}\right\Vert\le (r+\delta)(1-\gamma(A)),$$
for all $k\ge k_0$. Taking limit as $k$ goes to infinity:
$$
\limsup_k\left\Vert x_k-\frac{y_1+y_2}{ 2}\right\Vert\le (r+\delta)(1-\gamma(A))<r,
$$
which is a contradiction with the definition of $r$.
head: environment

label: diam
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{diam}
Assume that $X$ is endowed with a projection scheme $\mathcal{P}=\{P_n:1\le n\le \omega\}$ which is boundedly complete and $X$ is $\mathcal{P}$-AUC.   Then, the sequence of subsets  $\{Z(\{x_n\},C,\delta_s):s\in\mathbb{N}\}$, where $(\delta_s)$ is a nonnegative null sequence, is $\mathcal{P}$-asymptotically compact.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider $\alpha(\cdot)$ the Kuratowski measure of noncompactness. 
Notice that $\alpha(\cdot)$ is monotone and sublinear in the sense that
 $\alpha(Z_1)\le \alpha(Z_2)$ if $Z_1\subset Z_2$ and $\alpha(Z_1+Z_2)\le \alpha(Z_1)+\alpha(Z_2)$ for all sets $Z_1,Z_2$ in $X$. Additionally
$\alpha(Z)\le {\rm diam}(Z)$ for all $Z\subset X$.

Fix some $n\in\mathbb{N}$.
According to Definition \ref{kUC}, we can assume that  $P_n=A_n+B_n$  where $B_n$ is a finite-rank operator and $X$ is $\mathcal{A}$-UC for $\mathcal{A}=\{A_n: n\in \mathbb{N}\}$.
Notice that for all bounded set $Z\subset X$ we have that $P_n(Z)\subset A_n(Z)+B_n(Z)$ and $B_n(Z)$ is relatively compact. Hence, it suffices to show that

 $$\lim_{s}{\rm diam} \left(A_n(Z(\{x_n\},C,\delta_s)\right)=0$$
for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and this follows from Lemma \ref{gamma}.
head: environment

label: afps
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Take $(x_k)$ an a.f.p.s. in $C$.
It is enough to pick $y_s\in Z_s:=Z(\{x_k\},C,\delta_s)$ such that $\Vert y_s-T(y_s)\Vert <{1\over s} $ where $(\delta_s)$ is a decreasing sequence converging to 0,  apply Theorem \ref{diam} and the definition of $\mathcal{P}$-asymptotic compactness.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: If $X$ is a Banach space equipped with a projection scheme $\mathcal{P}$,  we say  that  $X$ has the $\mathcal{P}$-Schur property if every $\mathcal P$-convergent bounded sequence converges in norm.
head: environment

label: Schur
title: Corollary
body_md: \label{Schur} Let $X$ be a Banach space endowed with a projection scheme $\mathcal{P}$ which is $\mathcal{P}$-AUC and boundedly complete. If $X$ has the $\mathcal{P}$-Schur property, then $X$ has the FPP.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $C$ be a closed convex bounded subset, $T:C\to C$ nonexpansive and $(x_n)$ an afps in $C$ which is $\mathcal{P}$-convergent. If the $\mathcal{P}$-Schur property holds, then the norm limit of $(x_n)$ is a fixed point.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Given a Banach space with  a projection scheme $\mathcal{P}=\{P_k:k\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\omega\}\}$,  for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$ we
define
$$S(P_k):=\inf\{\limsup_n\Vert x_n+x\Vert: ((x_n),x)\in \mathcal{S}_1(X)\times S_X, P_k(x)=0\}.
$$
We say that $X$ is of  {\it $\mathcal{P}$-asymptotically  $\ell_1$-type} if
$$
S(\mathcal{P}):=\lim_k S(P_k)=2.
$$
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Given $k\in \mathbb{N}$, for every bounded sequence $(x_n)$ in $X$  $\mathcal{P}$-convergent to 0,  and for every $x\in X$ with $P_k(x)=0$, we have:
$$\limsup_n\Vert x_n+x\Vert \geq (S(P_k)-1)(\limsup_n\Vert x_n\Vert +\Vert x\Vert).$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $x=0$ or $\lim_n\Vert x_n\Vert=0$, the assertion is immediate. 
 
 Thus, we can assume $x\ne 0$ and  $l:=\limsup_n\Vert x_n\Vert>0$. Take a subsequence $(x_{n_s})$ such that $l:=\lim_s\Vert x_{n_s}\Vert$ and, without loss of generality, we can assume that $\Vert x_{n_s}\Vert\ne 0$ for all $s\in\mathbb{N}$, $\mathcal{P}-\lim_s {x_{n_s}\over \Vert x_{n_s}\Vert}=0$ and, given $\epsilon>0$ that

$$ \left\Vert \frac{x_{n_s}}{\Vert x_{n_s}\Vert }+\frac{x}{\Vert x\Vert}\right\Vert>S(P_k)-\epsilon.$$


Take $f_s\in X^*$ with $\Vert f_s\Vert=1$, such that
$$ \left\Vert \frac{x_{n_s}}{\Vert x_{n_s}\Vert }+\frac{x}{\Vert x\Vert}\right\Vert=f_s\left(\frac{x_{n_s}}{\Vert x_{n_s}\Vert }+\frac{x}{\Vert x\Vert}\right)=f_s\left(\frac{x_{n_s}}{\Vert x_{n_s}\Vert }\right)+f_s\left(\frac{x}{\Vert x\Vert}\right).$$
Then, $$f_s(x_{n_s}/\Vert x_{n_s}\Vert)\geq S(P_k)-\epsilon-1\quad {\rm and} \quad  f_s(x/\Vert x\Vert)\geq S(P_k)-\epsilon-1.$$

For all $s\in\mathbb{N}$, we have
$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\Vert x_{n_s}+x\Vert & \ge & f_s(x_{n_s}+x)
 =\Vert x_{n_s}\Vert f_s\left(\frac{x_{n_s}}{ \Vert x_{n_s}\Vert}\right)+\Vert x\Vert f_s\left(\frac{x}{ \Vert x\Vert}\right)\\
 &\ge & (S(P_k)-\epsilon-1)\left[\Vert x_{n_s}\Vert+\Vert x\Vert\right].\\
\end{array}
$$
Taking upper  limit when $s$ goes to infinity, the arbitrariness  of $\epsilon$ implies that
$$
\limsup_s\Vert x_{n_s}+x\Vert\ge (S(P_k)-1)\left[\lim_s\Vert x_{n_s}\Vert +\Vert x\Vert\right]= (S(P_k)-1)\left[\limsup_n\Vert x_{n}\Vert +\Vert x\Vert\right].
$$
Finally,
$$
\limsup_n\Vert x_n+x\Vert\ge \limsup_s\Vert x_{n_s}+x\Vert\ge (S(P_k)-1)\left[\limsup_n\Vert x_{n}\Vert +\Vert x\Vert\right]
$$
as we wanted to prove.
head: environment

label: bound
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

label: main
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\medskip

If $T$ has a fixed point, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise,  we can assume that
 $$
 \rho(C):=\inf\{\limsup_n\Vert x_n-x_0\Vert: \{(x_n)_n,x_0\}\in \mathcal{A}(C)\}>0,
 $$
After rescaling the norm, we may assume that $\rho(C)=1$.
\medskip

Take $s>0$ such that $\Delta(\mathcal{P})< s < {1\over 1+2K(\mathcal{P})}$.

\medskip

Define the function $a(\epsilon):=(1+2\epsilon)+K(\mathcal{P})2(1+\epsilon)$ for all $\epsilon>0$. Since $\lim_{\epsilon\to 0^+} a(\epsilon)s=[1+2K(\mathcal{P})]s<1$ we can fix some
 $\epsilon>0$  with
\begin{equation}\label{lambda}
a(\epsilon)s+(1+5\epsilon)<2.
\end{equation}


\medskip






Fix $\{(x_n),x_0\}\in\mathcal{A}(C)$ with
$$\limsup_n\Vert x_n-x_0\Vert< 1+\epsilon.$$

The above inequality
 implies that $\limsup_m\limsup_n\Vert x_n-x_m\Vert<2(1+\epsilon)$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that $\limsup_n\Vert x_n-x_m\Vert<2(1+\epsilon)$ for all $m\in\mathbb{N}$.
Set
$$
C_0:=\{z\in C: \limsup_n\Vert x_n-z\Vert\le 2(1+\epsilon)\},
$$
and we can assume that $(x_n)\subset C_0$. The set $C_0$ is a $T$-invariant, closed, convex, nonempty subset of $C$. Denote
$$
\rho(C_0):=\inf\{\limsup_n\Vert y_n-y_0\Vert: \{(y_n),y_0\}\in \mathcal{A}(C_0)\}\ge 1.
$$

 We will prove that there exists some $\{(y_n),y_0\}\in \mathcal{A}(C_0)$ such that
$$
r(\{y_n\},C_0)<2\rho(C_0)
$$
and this  will eventually lead to a contradiction.


\medskip

Since later we shall choose $k_0\in\mathbb{N}$ sufficiently large to satisfy some required conditions,   $X$ is of $\mathcal{P}$-asymptotically $\ell_1$-type,  we may assume without loss of generality that $S(P_k)>1$ for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$.


\medskip

 Take any  $\{(y_n),y_0\}\in\mathcal{A}(C_0)$. For $k\in\mathbb{N}$, we will  separately estimate the \lq\lq head''  $\Vert P_k(x_0-y_0)\Vert$ and the \lq\lq tail'' $\Vert (I-P_k)(x_0-y_0)\Vert$
 of the vector $ x_0-y_0$.

\medskip

First:

\begin{equation}\label{pk}
\begin{array}{rrl}
\Vert P_{k}(x_0-y_0)\Vert&=& \limsup_m\Vert P_{k}(x_0-y_m+y_m-y_0)\Vert\\
   & = &\limsup_m\Vert P_{k}(x_0-y_m)\Vert\\
 &= &\limsup_m\limsup_n \Vert P_{k}(x_0-x_n+x_n-y_m)\Vert\\
  &=&\limsup_m\limsup_n\Vert P_{k}(x_n-y_m)\Vert\\
  &\le & \Vert P_k\Vert \limsup_m\limsup_n\Vert x_n-y_m\Vert\le K(\mathcal{P})2(1+\epsilon).\\
\end{array}
\end{equation}


Next, using Lemma \ref{bound} we have:

\begin{equation}
\begin{array}{ll}
 & \displaystyle{ \Vert (I-P_k)(x_0-y_0)\Vert+\limsup_n\Vert y_n-y_0\Vert}\\
\le  &\displaystyle{ {1\over (S(P_k)-1)^2}\limsup_m\limsup_n\Vert x_n-y_m\Vert  }
 - \displaystyle{{1\over S(P_k)-1} \limsup_n\Vert x_n-x_0\Vert}   \\
 \le &\displaystyle{ {1\over (S(P_k)-1)^2}2(1+\epsilon) - {1\over S(P_k)-1} }.  \end{array}
\end{equation}
Thus,




\begin{equation}\label{Q}
\Vert (I-P_k)(x_0-y_0)\Vert+\limsup_n\Vert y_n-y_0\Vert\leq A_k:= \displaystyle{ {1\over (S(P_k)-1)^2}2(1+\epsilon) - {1\over S(P_k)-1} }.
\end{equation}
and $\lim_k A_k=1+2\epsilon$.



\medskip



Since $\mathcal{P}-\lim_n x_n=x_0$,  we have $\lim_n\Vert (I-P_\omega)(x_n-x_0)\Vert=0$ and consequently:
$$\limsup_n\Vert P_\omega(x_n-x_0)\Vert=\limsup_n\Vert x_n-x_0\Vert<1+\epsilon.$$
Fix $N_0\in\mathbb{N}$ with $x_{N_0}\in C_0$ and
$$
\Vert x_{N_0}-x_0\Vert <1+\epsilon;\ \Vert P_\omega(x_{N_0}-x_0)\Vert<1+\epsilon;\ \Vert (I-P_\omega)(x_{N_0}-x_0)\Vert<\epsilon.
$$


For every $k\in\mathbb{N}$ we have:
$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\Vert P_k(x_{N_0}-x_0)\Vert&\le &\Vert (P_k-P_\omega)(x_{N_0}-x_0)\Vert+ \Vert P_\omega(x_{N_0}-x_0)\Vert \\
 &\le & \Vert (P_k-P_\omega)(x_{N_0}-x_0)\Vert+1+\epsilon;
                                    \end{array}
$$
and
$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\Vert (I-P_{k})(x_{N_0}-x_0)\Vert&\le & \Vert (P_\omega-P_{k})(x_{N_0}-x_0)\Vert+\Vert (I-P_\omega)(x_{N_0}-x_0)\Vert\\
             &\le &\Vert (P_\omega-P_{k})(x_{N_0}-x_0)\Vert+\epsilon\\
             \end{array}.
$$



By the definition of a projection scheme (see Definition \ref{PS}.b)), the sequence $(P_k)_k$ converges pointwise to $P_\omega$.
Thus, we can take $k_0$ large enough so that $$\Vert (P_\omega-P_{k_0})(x_{N_0}-x_0)\Vert<\epsilon\quad  {\rm and} \quad A_{k_0}<1+3\epsilon.$$

Consequently, we deduce:
\begin{equation}\label{k}
\Vert P_{k_0}(x_{N_0}-x_0)\Vert<1+2\epsilon; \
\Vert (I-P_{k_0})(x_{N_0}-x_0)\Vert < 2\epsilon;
\end{equation}


\medskip

Then, for all $\{(y_n),y_0\}\in\mathcal{A}(C_0)$, we obtain:

\begin{equation}
\begin{array}{lll}
\Vert P_{k_0}(x_{N_0}-y_0)\Vert& \le & \Vert P_{k_0}(x_{N_0}-x_0)\Vert+ \Vert P_{k_0}(x_0-y_0)\Vert\\
    &\le & (1+2\epsilon)+K(\mathcal{P})2(1+\epsilon)=a(\epsilon),\\
    \end{array}
\end{equation}


and

\begin{equation}
\begin{array}{lll}\label{imp}
\Vert (I-P_{k_0})(x_{N_0}-y_0)\Vert +\limsup_n\Vert y_n-y_0\Vert &\le& \Vert (I-P_{k_0})(x_{N_0}-x_0)\Vert\\
&+ & \Vert (I-P_{k_0})(x_0-y_0)\Vert\\
&+&\limsup_n\Vert y_n-y_0\Vert\\
&\le & 2\epsilon+1+3\epsilon=1+5\epsilon.\\
\end{array}
\end{equation}

\medskip

Once  $x_{N_0}$ and $P_{k_0}$ have been fixed, the assumptions imply $\limsup_{\beta\to 0^+}{\Delta_{P_{k_0}(\beta)}\over \beta}\le \Delta(\mathcal{P})<s $ and there exists some $\beta_0\in(0,1)$ such that
$$
\Delta_{P_{k_0}}(\beta) <\beta s
$$
for every $\beta\le \beta_0$ and
\begin{equation}\label{beta}
\limsup_n\Vert x_n+\beta x\Vert\le 1+\beta s
\end{equation}
 for every $\{(x_n),x\}\in \mathcal{S}_1(X)\times S_X$ satisfying $P_k(x)=x$ and $\beta\in (0, \beta_0]$.



\medskip



Take $\lambda_0\in (0,1)$ such that $\lambda_0<{\beta_0\over a(\epsilon)}$.

\medskip

In particular, multiplying by $\lambda_0$ in (\ref{lambda}) and summing $2\rho(C_0)$ on each side of the equation we have:
$$
2\rho(C_0)+\lambda_0 a(\epsilon) s+\lambda_0(1+5\epsilon)<2\lambda_0 +2\rho(C_0) \le2\lambda_0 \rho(C_0)+2\rho(C_0).
$$
since $\rho(C_0)\ge 1$.
The above implies that:
$$
(2-2\lambda_0)\rho(C_0)+\lambda_0a(\epsilon)s+\lambda_0(1+5\epsilon)<2\rho(C_0).
$$
Take $t_0>0$ small enough so that
\begin{equation}\label{t0}
(2-2\lambda_0)(\rho(C_0)+t_0)+\lambda_0a(\epsilon)s+\lambda_0(1+5\epsilon)<2\rho(C_0).
\end{equation}


\medskip


Finally, take $((y_n),y_0)\in\mathcal{A}(C_0)$ with $r:=\limsup_n\Vert y_n-y_0\Vert\le \rho(C_0) + t_0$.


\medskip


  We have:
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
&\limsup_n\left\Vert y_n-y_0+\lambda_0 P_{k_0} (x_{N_0}-y_0)\right\Vert   \\
=& \displaystyle{r \limsup_n\left\Vert {y_n-y_0\over r}+{\lambda_0 \Vert P_{k_0} (x_{N_0}-y_0)\Vert \over r} {P_{k_0} (x_{N_0}-y_0)\over \Vert P_{k_0} (x_{N_0}-y_0)\Vert }\right\Vert}. \\
\end{array}
$$


\medskip

Notice that  $1\le r$ and  $\displaystyle{{\lambda_0 \Vert P_{k_0} (x_{N_0}-y_0)\Vert \over r}\le \lambda_0 a(\epsilon)<\beta_0.}$ Using (\ref{beta}) we deduce:




\begin{equation}\label{cota}
\begin{array}{lll}
\limsup_n\Vert y_n-y_0+\lambda_0 P_{k_0} (x_{N_0}-y_0)\Vert& \le & r\left[  1+{\lambda_0 \Vert P_{k_0} (x_{N_0}-y_0)\Vert\over r} s \right]\\
&= &\limsup_n\Vert y_n-y\Vert+\lambda_0  \Vert P_{k_0} (x_{N_0}-y_0)\Vert s\\
&\le & \limsup_n\Vert y_n-y\Vert+\lambda_0 a(\epsilon) s.\\
\end{array}
\end{equation}


\medskip

For all $n,m\in\mathbb{N}$,  we have:
\begin{equation}\label{cota2}
\begin{array}{lll}
\Vert y_n-(1-\lambda_0) y_m-\lambda_0 x_{N_0}\Vert&=&\Vert (y_n-y_0)-(1-\lambda_0) (y_m-y_0)-\lambda_0 (x_{N_0}-y_0)\Vert\\
& \le &
(1-\lambda_0)\Vert y_m-y_0\Vert +\Vert y_n-y_0-\lambda_0 P_{k_0}(x_{N_0}-y_0)\Vert\\
& +&\lambda_0 \Vert (I-P_{k_0})(x_{N_0}-y_0)\Vert.
\end{array}
\end{equation}




Taking limit as $n$ goes to infinity and using (\ref{cota}) and (\ref{cota2}):
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
& \limsup_n\Vert y_n-(1-\lambda_0) y_m-\lambda_0 x_{N_0}\Vert\\
\le & (1-\lambda_0)\Vert y_m-y_0\Vert+ \limsup_n\Vert y_n-y_0\Vert +\lambda_0 a(\epsilon) s+\lambda_0  \Vert (I-P_{k_0})(x_{N_0}-y_0)\Vert
\end{array}
$$

Taking limit when $m$ goes to infinity and using (\ref{imp}):
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
&\limsup_m \limsup_n\Vert y_n-(1-\lambda_0) y_m-\lambda_0 x_{N_0}\Vert\\
\le & (1-\lambda_0)\limsup_m\Vert y_m-y_0\Vert+ \limsup_n\Vert y_n-y_0\Vert+ \lambda_0 a(\epsilon) s\\
  +&\lambda_0 (1+5\epsilon-\limsup_n\Vert y_n-y_0\Vert).\\
\end{array}
$$

Consequently

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
& & \limsup_m\limsup_n\Vert y_n-(1-\lambda_0) y_m-\lambda_0 x_{N_0}\Vert\\
  & \le &   (2-2\lambda_0)\limsup_n\Vert y_n-y_0\Vert+   \lambda_0 a(\epsilon) s  +\lambda_0 (1+5\epsilon) \\
  &\le & (2-2\lambda_0)(\rho(C_0)+t_0)+  \lambda_0 a(\epsilon) s  +\lambda_0 (1+5\epsilon)\\
  &<&2\rho(C_0);\\
\end{array}
$$
where we have used (\ref{t0}).

\medskip

Choose $\alpha<2\rho(C_0)$  such that
$$\limsup_m\limsup_n\Vert y_n-(1-\lambda_0) y_m-\lambda_0 x_{N_0}\Vert<\alpha$$
and  $m\in\mathbb{N}$ with
$$
\limsup_n\Vert y_n-(1-\lambda_0) y_m-\lambda_0 x_{N_0}\Vert\le \alpha<2\rho(C_0).
$$
Since $(1-\lambda_0) y_m+\lambda_0 x_{N_0}\in C_0$ by convexity, we deduce that the set
$$
C_1:=\{ z\in C_0: \limsup_n\Vert y_n-z\Vert\le \alpha\}
$$
is closed, convex, $T$-invariant and nonempty. Take $\{(z_n), z_0\}\in \mathcal{A}(C_1)$. Using again inequality (\ref{dl}) we have:
$$
\begin{array}{lll}
2\rho(C_0)&>& \alpha\ge \limsup_m\limsup_n\Vert y_n-z_m\Vert\\
   & \ge & \limsup_n\Vert y_n-y_0\Vert+\limsup_m\Vert z_m-z_0\Vert\ge 2\rho(C_0).
\end{array}
$$

The above contradiction implies  that $T$ has a fixed point, as we wanted to prove.
head: environment

label: sum
title: Theorem
body_md: \label{sum} Let $X=(\ell_1,\vert\vert\vert\cdot \vert\vert\vert)\oplus_2 \ell_2$, where the norm $\vert\vert\vert \cdot\vert\vert\vert$ is given by (\ref{Linnorm}). Then $X$ has the FPP.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We fix some notation. For $x\in X$ we write $x=x^1+x^2$ where $x^1\in\ell_1$ and $x^2\in \ell_2$. Let $(R_n)_n$ be the  projections on $\ell_1$ associated to its canonical Schauder basis.
 We define a projection scheme on $X$ in the following way: we set $P_\omega=I$, the identity on X, and for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ we define the projection:  $P_n(x)=P_n(x^1+x^2):=R_n(x^1)+x^2$. Then $\mathcal{P}:=\{P_n: 1\le n\le \omega\}$ is a projection scheme which is boundedly complete.

 We prove that $\mathcal{P}$ satisfies the remaining assumptions of Theorem \ref{main}.

Observe that $P_n=R_n+I_2$  where $I_2(x^1+x^2)=x^2$ and every $R_n$ has finite rank. Furthermore, $X$ is $\mathcal{A}$-UC where $\mathcal{A}$  consists solely of the projection $I_2$, since the direct sum is endowed with the $\ell_2$-norm (see Example \ref{puc}).

\medskip

Additionally,  $X$ is of $\mathcal{P}$-asymptotically $\ell_1$-type:  Indeed,  let $(x_n)$ be a $\mathcal{P}$-null sequence with $\limsup_n\Vert x_n\Vert=1$. In particular $\lim_n R_k(x_n^1)=0$ for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\lim_n I_2(x_n^2)=x_n^2=0$. Consequently, $(x_n^1)$ is  coordinatewise convergent to 0  and we can assume, taking a subsequence and  without loss of generality, that $(x_n^1)$ is a block basic sequence.

 Take $x=x^1+x^2\in S_X$ with $P_k(x^1+x^2)=R_k(x^1) +I_2(x^2)=0$. Thus  $x^2=0$ and
 $$
\begin{array}{lll}
\limsup_n\Vert x_n+x\Vert&=&\limsup_n\Vert (I-P_k)(x_n)+x\Vert\\
                &=&\limsup_n\vert\vert\vert (I-R_k)(x_n^1)+x^1\vert\vert\vert\\
                                  & \ge & \gamma_k \left(\limsup_n\vert\vert\vert  (I-R_k)(x_n^1)\vert\vert\vert+ \vert\vert\vert x^1\vert\vert\vert\right)\\
                                  & = & \gamma_k \left(\limsup_n\Vert  x_n\Vert + \Vert x\Vert\right)=2\gamma_k\\
                                  \end{array},
$$
which shows that $S(P_k)\ge 2\gamma_k$ and  $X$ is of $\mathcal{P}$-asymptotically $\ell_1$ type (see \cite{todos}).

\medskip


We next prove that $\limsup_{\lambda\to 0^+}{\Delta_{P_k}(\lambda)\over \lambda}=0$ for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$, which implies that $\Delta(\mathcal{P})=0$.

 Fix $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and let $x=x^1+x^2\in X$ with $P_k(x)=x$ and $\Vert x\Vert=1$. Consider $(x_n)$ a $\mathcal{P}$-null convergent sequence with $\limsup_n\Vert x_n\Vert=1$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that $x_n=x_n^1$ with $(x_n^1)$ a weak$^*$-convergent sequence in $\ell_1$ and $\limsup_n \vert\vert\vert x_n^1\vert\vert\vert =1$. Let $0<\lambda<{1\over \gamma_k}-1$. Then
$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\limsup_n\Vert x_n+\lambda x\Vert^2&= &\lambda^2\Vert x^2\Vert^2+\limsup_n\vert\vert\vert x_n^1+\lambda x^1\vert\vert\vert^2\\
& =& \lambda^2\Vert x^2\Vert^2+ \limsup_n \vert\vert\vert x_n^1\vert\vert\vert^2\le   \lambda^2+1,\\
\end{array}
$$
 which implies $\limsup_n\Vert x_n+\lambda x\Vert\le  (\lambda^2+1)^{1\over 2}$ and $\Delta_{P_k}(\lambda)\le (\lambda^2+1)^{1\over 2}-1$ for $0<\lambda <{1\over \gamma_k}-1$.
Therefore
$$
\limsup_{\lambda\to 0^+}{\Delta_{P_k}(\lambda)\over \lambda}=0.
$$
All the assumptions of Theorem  \ref{main} are satisfied and we can conclude that $X$ has the FPP.

label: uciso
title: Corollary
body_md: \label{uciso} Every uniformly convex Banach space $Y$ can be isometrically embedded in a nonreflexive Banach space with the FPP.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Define
$X:=(\ell_1,\vert\vert\vert\cdot \vert\vert\vert)\oplus_2 Y$. Using the same arguments as in Theorem \ref{sum}, we can prove the FPP from Theorem \ref{main}.
head: environment

label: ss
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{ss} Let $X$ be a Banach space with a  Schauder basis and denote $(P_k)$ the standard projections. The norm of $X$ is called near-infinity concentrated (n.i.c.) if it has the following properties:

\begin{itemize}

\item[(1)]
It is a sequentially separating norm.

\item[(2)] It is a premonotone norm.


\item[(3)]  There exist $R_0>5$ and $M\in [0,1)$ such that for every $k\in \mathbb{N}$, there exists a function $F_k:(0,\infty) \to [0, \infty)$ satisfying the following conditions:
\begin{itemize}

\item[(a)] $\lim_{\lambda\to 0^+} F_k(\lambda) \leq M/R_0$.

\item[(b)]

For every bounded pointwise-null sequence $(x_n)$ with $\liminf_n \Vert x_n \Vert  \geq 1$, for all $\lambda\in (0,\infty)$, and for every $z\in X$ with  $P_k(z)=z$ and $\Vert z\Vert \leq R_0$, we have
$$\limsup_n \Vert x_n+\lambda z\Vert \leq \limsup \Vert x_n\Vert +F_k(\lambda) \Vert z\Vert.$$
\end{itemize}\end{itemize}
head: environment

label: castillo
title: Theorem
body_md: \label{castillo} Let $X$ be a Banach space with a boundedly complete Schauder basis and  a near-infinity concentrated (n.i.c.) norm on X. Then $X$ has the FPP.
head: environment

label: failure
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{failure} Let $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a $\sigma$-finite  measure space and $p: \Omega\to [1,\infty]$
a
measurable function. Assume that one of the following conditions holds:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)]  $p_+(\Omega\setminus \Omega_\infty)=+\infty$;

\item[(ii)]
 The set $\Omega_1$
 either contains a nonatomic set with positive measure or
infinitely many atoms;

\item[(iii)]


 The set $\Omega_\infty$
 either contains a nonatomic set with positive measure
or infinitely many atoms .

\end{itemize}
Then $L^{p(\cdot)}(\Omega)$ fails to have the FPP.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We will check that $\ell_1$  is contained isometrically
in $L^{p(\cdot)}(\Omega)$ whenever one of the above assertions holds. Indeed,
an isometric copy of $\ell_\infty$  can be found in case that (i) holds (see \cite[Theorem 2.3]{DJ}) and $\ell_\infty$  contains an
isometric copy of every separable Banach space. When (ii) holds, an isometric
copy of $L_1([0,1])$ can be given whenever a nonatomic set with positive measure exists
or, simply,  an isometric copy of $\ell_1$ can be formed with infinitely many atoms.
Likewise, we arrive at the same conclusion whenever (iii) holds.
head: environment

label: PSV
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{PSV}  Assume that  $p_+(\Omega\setminus \Omega_\infty) <\infty$ and the set $\Omega_1\cup\Omega_\infty$ only contains finitely many atoms.
Define $P_n(f)=f\cdot 1_{\{\gamma_n\leq p\le \infty\}}$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$  and $P_\omega(f)=f\cdot 1_{\{1< p\le \infty\}}$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: $\mathcal{P}=\{P_n: 1\le n\le \omega\}$ is a  premonotone projection scheme which is boundedly complete.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It is clear that $P_n\circ P_m=P_{\min\{n,m\}}$ if $n<m\le \omega$ and that $I-P_\omega$ has rank in a finite-dimensional closed subspace, since $\Omega_1$ is formed  by just finitely many atoms at most.
To prove $\lim_n \Vert P_n(f)-P_\omega(f)\Vert=\lim_n \Vert f\cdot 1_{\{1<p<\gamma_n\}}\Vert=0$,  observe that $(f\cdot 1_{\{1<p<\gamma_n\}})_n$ is a monotonous sequence converging to zero almost everywhere. Since $p_+(\Omega\setminus \Omega_\infty) <\infty$  the convergence for the modulus implies the convergence for the norm. It is trivial that $\Vert I-P_n\Vert\le 1$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$.


\medskip

 To prove bounded completeness, consider a bounded sequence  $(f_n)_n$  in  $L^{p(\cdot)}(\Omega)$, say $\Vert f_n\Vert \leq M$ for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$, such that $P_n(f_m)=f_n$ for $m\geq n$.  In particular $P_n(f_n)=f_n$ which implies that $supp(f_n)\subset \{\gamma_n<p\le \infty\}$.
The above implies that, defining $f(t)=f_n(t)$ whether $p(t)\geq \gamma_n$, we obtain a well-defined measurable function on $\{1<p\le +\infty\}$.
Moreover, the sequence $\{P_n(f)\}_n=\{f \cdot 1_{\{\gamma_n<p\le +\infty\}}\}_n$  is nondecreasing and convergent to $f$ almost everywhere. From the Monotone Convergence Theorem and Lemma \ref{properties} we obtain   $$\rho(f/M)=\lim_n \rho(P_n(f)/M)\le \limsup_n\rho(f_n/M) \leq 1$$ and so $f$ belongs to  $L^{p(\cdot)}(\Omega)$.
head: environment

label: kUC2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{kUC2}
$L^{p(\cdot)}(\Omega)$ is $\mathcal{P}$-AUC
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Notice that for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ we can write $P_n=A_n+B_n$ where $A_n(f)=f\cdot 1_{\{\gamma_n\leq p< \infty\}}$ and $B_n(f)=f \cdot 1_{\Omega_\infty}$. It is clear that $B_n$ has finite-rank for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Let us prove that $L^{p(\cdot)}(\Omega)$ is $\mathcal{A}$-UC where $\mathcal{A}=\{A_n: n\in\mathbb{N}\}$.

\medskip






 Let  $\rho_n:L^{p(\cdot)}(\Omega)\to [0,\infty]$ be the modular defined by
$$\rho_n(f)=\rho(A_n(f))=\int_{\{\gamma_n\le p <+\infty\}} \vert f(t)\vert^{p(t)}dt.$$ Since $p_+(\Omega\setminus \Omega_\infty)<\infty$,  we can use the uniform convexity of the  modular $\rho_n$ given by Lemma \ref{ucc2}. Hence, for a given  $\delta>0$, there exists some $\alpha_n>0$ (depending on $\gamma_n, \delta $ and $p_+(\Omega\setminus \Omega_\infty))$ such that
$$
\rho_n\left(\frac{f+g}{ 2}\right)\le \frac{\rho_n(f)+\rho_n(g)}{ 2}-\alpha_n
$$
whenever $\Vert A_n(f-g)\Vert>\delta$ and $\Vert A_n(f)\Vert\le \Vert f\Vert \le 1$ and $\Vert A_n(g)\Vert\le \Vert g\Vert\le 1$.

\vskip 0.5cm
Using the additivity of the modular   and Proposition \ref{properties} we deduce
$$
\rho\left(\frac{f+g}{ 2}\right)\le \frac{\rho(f)+\rho(g)}{2}-\alpha_n\le 1-\alpha_n.
$$
and
$$\left\Vert \frac{f+g}{ 2}\right\Vert\le (1-\alpha_n)^{\frac{1}{ p_+(\Omega\setminus \Omega_\infty)}}=1-(1-\alpha_n)^{\frac{1}{ p_+(\Omega\setminus \Omega_\infty)}},
$$
and the proof is complete.
head: environment

label: gammaa
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{gammaa} Assume $1 < \gamma<\infty$ and let $f,g\in L^{p(\cdot)}(\Omega)$  be normalized disjointedly supported functions with support in $\{1\le p\leq \gamma\}$. Then:
$$
\Vert f+g\Vert\ge 2^{\frac{1}{\gamma}}
$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $r=2^{1/\gamma}$. Since $r>1$ we have
$$ \rho\left(\frac{g}{r}\right)=\int_\Omega \left(\frac{1}{r}\right)^{p(t)} \vert g(t)\vert^{p(t)} d\mu \geq  \left(\frac{1}{r}\right)^\gamma\int_\Omega \vert g(t)\vert^{p(t)} d\mu
=\left(\frac{1}{r}\right)^\gamma.$$
Likewise $\rho(f)\geq  \left(\frac{1}{r}\right)^\gamma$ and
since $f$ and $g$ are disjointly supported we have
$$
\rho\left(\frac{f+g}{ r}\right)=\rho\left(\frac{f}{ r}\right) +\rho\left(\frac{g}{ r}\right)\geq
\left(1 \over r\right)^{\gamma} +\left(1\over r\right)^{\gamma}=1
$$
and, using Lemma \ref{properties},  the proof is complete.
head: environment

label: SS2
title: Lemma
body_md: \label{SS2}  $L^{p(\cdot)}(\Omega)$  is  of $\mathcal{P}$-asymptotically $\ell_1$-type.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix  $k\in \mathbb{N}$. We will prove that $S(P_k)\geq 2^{\frac{1}{\gamma_k}}$ and
 passing to the limit as  $k\to \infty$,
we obtain that $S(\mathcal{P})=2$. Consider any $\{(f_n),f\}\in  \mathcal{S}_1(X) \times S_X$ with $X=L^{p(\cdot)}(\Omega)$ and $P_k(f) = 0$. That means, in particular, that supp$\,(f)\subset \{1<t<\gamma_k\}\cup \Omega_1$ and $\lim_n\Vert f_n\cdot 1_{\Omega_1}\Vert=0$ (see Definition \ref{Pconvergence}).

\medskip

Note that  the following equality holds:
$$
\limsup_n\left\Vert f_n-\frac{(I-P_k)(f_n)}{\Vert (I-P_k)(f_n)\Vert}\right\Vert=0,
$$
and
$$\limsup_n\Vert  f_n+f\Vert = \limsup_n\left \Vert \frac{(I-P_k)(f_n)}{\Vert (I-P_k)(f_n)\Vert} +f\right\Vert\ge 2^{1\over \gamma_k}
$$
 following the inequality in Lemma \ref{gammaa}.
head: environment

label: lambda2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lambda2}
Given $\gamma>1$, the following holds:  for all normalized $f,g\in L^{p(\cdot)}(\Omega)$  disjointly supported functions with $supp(g)\subset\{\gamma\le p\le \infty \}$ we have
$$
\Vert f+\lambda g\Vert\le 1+\lambda^\gamma
$$
for $\lambda\in (0,1)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $p_+(\Omega\setminus \Omega_\infty)<\infty$,   we have $\rho(f)=1=\rho(g)$ according to Lemma \ref{properties}. Set $r:=1+\lambda^\gamma>1$. Then, we have
$$
\rho\left(\frac{f+\lambda g}{r}\right)=\rho\left(\frac{f}{ r} \right)+\rho\left(\frac{\lambda g}{r}\right)\le
 \frac{1}{ r}\rho(f)+ \frac{1}{ r}\rho(\lambda g)\le  \frac{1}{ r}(1+\lambda^\gamma)   =1.
$$
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: For all $k\in \mathbb{N}$, we have $\Delta_{P_k}(\lambda)\leq \lambda^{\gamma_k}$. In particular  $\Delta(\mathcal{P})=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume that $\{(f_n),f\}\in \mathcal{S}_1(X)\times S_X$ and $P_k(f)=f$. We have that supp$\, (f)\subset \{\gamma_k\le p\le \infty\}$ and supp$\, (I-P_k)(f_n) \subset \{1<p<\gamma_k\}$. By Lemma  \ref{lambda2} and the $\mathcal{P}$-convergence we have:
$$\limsup_n \Vert f_n+\lambda f\Vert = \limsup_n \Vert (I-P_k)(f_n)+\lambda f\Vert  \leq 1+\lambda^{\gamma_k}.
$$
The above implies that $\lim_{\lambda\to 0^+}{\Delta_{P_k}(\lambda)\over \lambda}=0$ and this holds for every $k\in\mathbb{N}$ so $\Delta(\mathcal{P})=0$.
head: environment

label: main2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{main2}
Assume that $(\Omega,\Sigma, \mu)$ is a $\sigma$-finite measure space $p_+(\Omega\setminus\Omega_\infty) <\infty$ and the set $\Omega_1\cup\Omega_\infty$ only contains finitely many atoms. Then $L^{p(\cdot)}(\Omega)$ has the FPP.
head: environment

label: co
title: Corollary
head: environment
